whyThisMatters: In the first minute of a real incident, most people freeze or try to fix it alone. The habit that helps you is knowing your next step before you need it.
rememberThis: STOP, VERIFY, REPORT. Use this order every time, no matter what the situation looks like.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group what they would do in the first few seconds of each scenario. Ask before you show the good answer.
For the phone call case, ask if anyone has a trusted number they know by heart to call back on. Or would they need to look it up under pressure?
Ask why "wait and see if anything goes wrong" feels tempting, even though it is the wrong choice in every case here.
Ask how it felt to decide under time pressure. Was it harder to pause when the clock was running?
For the CFO video call case, ask if anyone would feel okay ending a call with a senior leader to go and check.
Ask the group to name their own trusted way to check an urgent request. Do this for each role here: Finance, HR, Operations, and Offshore.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is trying to fix it yourself before reporting. People change their own password, restart a locked device, or move a leaked folder. It feels helpful. But it often destroys evidence that IT needs. People also most often get the CFO video call wrong, choosing "approve the payment" because the face and voice matched — a live call feels harder to fake than an email.

cases.title: You Clicked a Phishing Link
cases.scenario: You are checking candidate emails. You click a link in what looked like a normal follow-up. After you click, the page looks wrong.

decisions.prompt: The page that opened looks strange. A fake login box appears. What do you do first?

options.text: Type your work login to see if it is real
options.feedback: Do not type your login on a strange page. Even a quick test can give away your password.

options.text: Close the tab without typing anything and leave the device alone
options.feedback: Right choice. Not typing anything stops the attack. Leaving the device as it is keeps what IT needs to see.

options.text: Take a screenshot to show a coworker before you do anything else
options.feedback: Sharing it with coworkers slows you down. The most important step is to tell IT fast, not to ask others first.

cases.debrief: Whether it is a link, an attachment, or anything unexpected, the steps are the same. STOP before you do more. Do not touch the device more than you need to. REPORT right away with details. Every minute you wait is a minute IT does not have.

cases.title: The Payroll Details Text
cases.scenario: A coworker gets a text "from HR" asking them to click a link and update their payroll details immediately.

options.text: Click the link and update your details quickly so payroll isn't delayed
options.feedback: Clicking an unverified link to "update" payroll details is exactly how these texts steal a login — a payroll deadline is never worth that risk.

options.text: Don't click — check your details directly through the official HR portal, and report the text
options.feedback: Right call. Going straight to a channel you already trust removes the attacker's link from the equation entirely, and reporting it helps flag the pattern for others.

options.text: Reply to the text asking if it's really from HR
options.feedback: Replying only confirms your number is active — it doesn't verify anything, since a scam text will just say yes.

cases.debrief: STOP - do not click. VERIFY using the official HR portal or a known contact. REPORT it to IT or security.

cases.title: You Found an Unknown USB Drive
cases.scenario: You are walking on deck and find a USB drive taped to a computer. It has no label and no clear owner.

decisions.prompt: No one says it is theirs and you are curious. What do you do?

options.text: Plug it into a nearby workstation to check what's on it
options.feedback: Unknown drives can run harmful code as soon as they are plugged in. Plugging it in just to look is how it gets in.

options.text: Leave it unplugged and don't try to identify the owner yourself
options.feedback: Correct. Not plugging it in removes the risk. It is not your job to find out who owns it.

options.text: Ask around the crew mess if anyone's missing a USB drive
options.feedback: This feels helpful, but it wastes time. Word can also reach the person who left it there before IT sees it.

cases.debrief: Unknown USB drives are an easy way for harmful software to get into a system. STOP before you plug anything in. Check with IT how to handle it safely. REPORT it directly so it is checked properly, not left in a drawer.

cases.title: The CFO Video Call
cases.scenario: You are on a video call with someone who looks and sounds exactly like your CFO. Their picture freezes for a second and the lighting looks a little off. But they speak with full confidence. They ask you to approve an unusual payment right now, before the call ends.

options.text: Approve the payment - the face and voice matched, so it must really be them
options.feedback: A real-looking face and voice on a call is not proof of identity. Both can be faked. An unusual, urgent payment is exactly when to STOP and VERIFY using a channel you already trust. Never use a channel given to you in the same call. Then REPORT anything strange.

options.text: Quietly stall by saying you'll do it after the call, hoping they forget
options.feedback: A real-looking face and voice on a call is not proof of identity. Both can be faked. An unusual, urgent payment is exactly when to STOP and VERIFY using a channel you already trust. Never use a channel given to you in the same call. Then REPORT anything strange.

options.text: End the call and verify the request by contacting your CFO through a number or channel you already know is real
options.feedback: Correct. A real-looking face and voice on a call is not proof. An unusual, urgent payment is exactly when to STOP and VERIFY using a channel you already trust. Never use a channel given to you in the same call. Then REPORT anything strange.

options.text: Ask a coworker in chat if they got the same request, then decide
options.feedback: A real-looking face and voice on a call is not proof of identity. Both can be faked. An unusual, urgent payment is exactly when to STOP and VERIFY using a channel you already trust. Never use a channel given to you in the same call. Then REPORT anything strange.

cases.debrief: A convincing face and voice is not proof of identity — treat an unusual, urgent request the same on video as you would over email: STOP, VERIFY through a channel you already trust, REPORT.

cases.title: Your Laptop Was Stolen
cases.scenario: You are back from a site visit and notice your work laptop was taken from the van during a stop.

decisions.prompt: You just noticed it is gone. What do you do first?

options.text: Drive back to the last stop to look for it yourself
options.feedback: Every minute you spend searching is a minute IT is not locking accounts or wiping the device. Speed matters more than searching.

options.text: Report it to IT Security and your manager immediately
options.feedback: Correct. Fast reporting lets IT act while there is still time to lock things.

cases.debrief: A stolen device with company access is a race against time. STOP trying to find it yourself. REPORT right away with what you know. Check that the next steps happened, like remote lock and password changes.

cases.title: The Candidate Attachment
cases.scenario: A message looks like it is from your usual hiring site. It forwards a promising candidate CV as an attachment. But the sender address is spelled a little differently than normal. It says the candidate needs an answer "within the hour" or they will take another offer.

options.text: Open the attachment quickly so you don't lose a strong candidate
options.feedback: A small spelling change in the sender address plus fake urgency is a classic trap. Attackers know HR often gets attachments from strangers. STOP, VERIFY, and REPORT applies to a "candidate" file just like any other email.

options.text: Reply to the sender asking for more information
options.feedback: A small spelling change in the sender address plus fake urgency is a classic trap. Attackers know HR often gets attachments from strangers. STOP, VERIFY, and REPORT applies to a "candidate" file just like any other email.

options.text: STOP before opening anything, VERIFY the sender's exact email address and the platform directly, then REPORT if it doesn't check out
options.feedback: A small spelling change in the sender address plus fake urgency is a classic trap. Attackers know HR often gets attachments from strangers. STOP, VERIFY, and REPORT applies to a "candidate" file just like any other email.

options.text: Forward it to a colleague and let them decide
options.feedback: A small spelling change in the sender address plus fake urgency is a classic trap. Attackers know HR often gets attachments from strangers. STOP, VERIFY, and REPORT applies to a "candidate" file just like any other email.

cases.debrief: A misspelled sender address plus manufactured urgency is a classic lure — HR inboxes get attachments from strangers routinely, so STOP, VERIFY, REPORT applies here just like anywhere else.

cases.title: You Suspect a Data Breach
cases.scenario: You see financial files that should not be open to everyone. They are now in a shared folder anyone can open.

decisions.prompt: You just spotted this. What do you do first?

options.text: Message a few colleagues to see if they've noticed it too
options.feedback: Telling others, even inside the company, can spread details before IT has checked what happened.

options.text: Avoid discussing it publicly or on social media, and don't touch the files
options.feedback: Correct. Not talking about it widely and not touching files keeps the evidence safe.

cases.debrief: A possible data leak is like a scene you should not touch. STOP before you talk about it or try to fix it. Note what you saw without changing anything. REPORT right away so the trained team can take over.

cases.title: Skip the Permit Sign-Off?
cases.scenario: You get a Teams message from someone you do not know. No photo, no chat history. They say the site supervisor cannot be reached. They ask you to skip the permit-to-work sign-off on a job "just this once" so the schedule does not slip.

options.text: It's fine - schedules matter, and you can sort out the paperwork later
options.feedback: An unknown sender, time pressure, and a request to skip a safety check are the warning signs. Skipping a check because an urgent, unreachable person said so is the red flag. It is the same pattern as a fake CEO asking for a wire transfer. Here it targets a safety step instead of money.

options.text: Someone with no verified identity is pressuring you to skip a safety check, using urgency and unreachability as the excuse
options.feedback: Correct. An unknown sender, time pressure, and a request to skip a safety check are the warning signs. Skipping a check because an urgent, unreachable person said so is the red flag. It is the same pattern as a fake CEO asking for a wire transfer. Here it targets a safety step instead of money.

options.text: It's a normal, routine reminder about the schedule
options.feedback: An unknown sender, time pressure, and a request to skip a safety check are the warning signs. Skipping a check because an urgent, unreachable person said so is the red flag. It is the same pattern as a fake CEO asking for a wire transfer. Here it targets a safety step instead of money.

options.text: It's expected - supervisors often message from other accounts
options.feedback: An unknown sender, time pressure, and a request to skip a safety check are the warning signs. Skipping a check because an urgent, unreachable person said so is the red flag. It is the same pattern as a fake CEO asking for a wire transfer. Here it targets a safety step instead of money.

cases.debrief: An unverified sender plus time pressure plus a request to bypass a normal control is the same pattern as a fake-boss scam — just aimed at a safety process instead of a wire transfer.

cases.title: You Got a Suspicious Phone Call
cases.scenario: Someone calls the ship phone and says they are from head office IT. They ask you to confirm your login details by phone.

decisions.prompt: The caller wants you to confirm your login details right now. What do you do?

options.text: Give a partial answer to seem cooperative without giving everything
options.feedback: Even a small hint can be enough. The caller only needs one true detail to build the rest.

options.text: Decline to give out any passwords, codes, or personal information
options.feedback: Correct. A real IT request will never ask you to say your password on an incoming call.

cases.debrief: Urgency on a call is a trick, not a real deadline. STOP before you share anything. Check by calling back on a number you trust. REPORT the attempt so others can be warned.

cases.title: Your Screen Just Locked
cases.scenario: A message covers your screen and asks for payment to unlock your files. A countdown timer is running.

options.text: Try to pay quickly before the timer runs out
options.feedback: Paying does not guarantee you get files back. It also funds the next attack. And you skip reporting, which is what IT needs most.

options.text: Disconnect the device from the network immediately
options.feedback: Right idea. This can stop it from spreading to other systems before IT steps in.

options.text: Post about it in the team chat to warn others
options.feedback: This is understandable, but it is not the fastest way to contain it. It can also cause panic before IT knows the scope.

cases.debrief: Ransomware wants you to panic and pay. STOP by disconnecting right away. Do not try to pay or fix it yourself. REPORT fast so IT can stop it from reaching other systems.
